analysis: Most of the PR is documentation and tests (changelog.d/sandbox-setup-resize.md, cli-reference.md, sandboxes.md, SandboxSetupTests, SandboxTestSupport). The production changes are SandboxEligibility.swift (display-only free-space arithmetic and note), SandboxSetupProgress.swift (confirm defaultYes) and SandboxSetupCommand.swift (replay not visible here). The security-relevant change is that `darkbloom sandbox setup` on an already-set-up Mac now downloads install.sh on every run, runs it with `--plan`, compares the slot counts, and may rerun the installer to apply the plan. This reuses the TB-013/T-061 download-and-run-as-owner path (A-019) more often, but adds no new class of trust. The docs and tests state these controls: the HTTPS-only URL, 1 MiB cap, shebang check and 0600/0700 staging are unchanged; `--force` is never passed, so running jobs are not stopped; exit 4 is surfaced; the check is skipped while jobs run. SandboxSlotChange interpolates only Ints and Sandbox.cli, so there is no injection. Plan counts come from the installer's own output, so a hostile installer is already inside the T-061 exposure. I considered, and did not report, the unattended path: with --yes or no terminal, setup applies a plan that adds slots and removes none, and the docs describe this intentionally. It is a design decision within the existing trust model, not a regression. Not verifiable here: the SandboxSetupCommand.swift source (line citations from the source pass could not be checked), SandboxSlotChange.onlyAdds correctness, and whether the installer's release verification is unchanged. The TB-013/T-061 text could note the recurring re-plan download. No effect on coordinator, attestation, TB-012 or the T-041 cache.

findings.detail: SandboxTerminal.confirm now takes defaultYes. At head line 463 it returns true when defaultYes && answer.isEmpty. readInput() returns nil at EOF (Ctrl-D, closed stdin, exhausted pipe), and `?? ""` turns that into an empty answer, so EOF counts as approval instead of requiring a real Enter. The new already-set-up prompt (`Apply? [Y/n]`) uses this path. Per the docs, the prompt appears when the plan's counts differ from the installed ones, including plans that remove slots. Applying runs the freshly downloaded install.sh as the Mac owner and restarts the add-on (TB-013, T-061, A-019). A stray EOF, or a wrapper that has a pty but closes stdin early, can therefore apply a slot-removing change with no explicit answer. Fix: treat a nil read as no, for example `guard let line = readInput() else { return false }`, and apply the default only to an explicitly entered empty line.
findings.title: Default-yes confirm treats EOF/closed stdin as consent to a slot-changing installer run
